test_title: PYST 23: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 08 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: A car driver uses a concave mirror as a shaving mirror at home. If his face is kept close to the mirror, how will the image formed be?

options.text: Real, inverted, and larger than the face
Real, inverted, and smaller than the face

solution:
The correct answer is __**Virtual, erect, and magnified**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Concave mirrors** are spherical mirrors with a reflecting surface that curves inward. They are capable of forming both real and virtual images based on the object's position relative to the mirror's focal point.
 
• When a person's face is placed **close to a concave mirror** (i.e., within its focal length), the mirror produces a **virtual, erect, and magnified image**. This happens because the reflected rays appear to diverge, and the image is formed on the same side as the object.
 
• For a concave mirror, the nature of the image depends on the **object's position**:
 
 
• When the object is beyond the center of curvature, the image is real, inverted, and smaller.
 
• When the object is at the focal point, no image is formed as the reflected rays are parallel.
 
• When the object is within the focal length, as in the case of shaving mirrors, the image is virtual, erect, and magnified.
 
 
 
• Shaving mirrors are typically designed to have a **short focal length**, ensuring that the face is within the focal length of the mirror to produce a magnified image. This feature allows the user to see a clear and enlarged reflection of their face for precise grooming.
 
• **Magnification** occurs because the reflected rays diverge as if they are originating from a point behind the mirror, creating a larger virtual image.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Uses of Concave Mirrors:**

 
 
• In **shaving mirrors** to produce a magnified and clear image of the face.
 
• In **telescopes** to gather and focus light from distant objects.
 
• In **dentistry**, dentists use concave mirrors to view an enlarged image of teeth for better diagnosis.
 
• In **headlights and flashlights**, concave mirrors are used to focus light into a beam.
 
 
 
• **Key Characteristics of Concave Mirrors:**
 
 
• They have a **real focus** (light rays converge at the focal point).
 
• Their reflective surface is on the inner side of the spherical shape.
 
• The type of image they form depends on the **object's position** relative to the focal point and center of curvature.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Convex Mirrors:**
 
 
• **Concave mirrors** can form real and virtual images, while **convex mirrors** always produce virtual, erect, and diminished images.
 
• Convex mirrors are used as **rear-view mirrors** in vehicles because they provide a wide field of view.
 
 
 
• **Image Formation by Concave Mirrors:**
 
 
• Beyond the center of curvature: Real, inverted, and smaller than the object.
 
• At the center of curvature: Real, inverted, and the same size as the object.
 
• Between the center of curvature and the focal point: Real, inverted, and magnified.
 
• At the focal point: No image is formed (rays are parallel).
 
• Within the focal length: Virtual, erect, and magnified.
 
 
 
• **Practical Applications:**
 
 
• Concave mirrors are widely used in optical instruments, scientific equipment, and daily-use tools like shaving mirrors and makeup mirrors.
 
• They are also used in solar devices, such as **solar cookers**, to focus sunlight for heating purposes.
